01The premise

Generation is easy. Finishing is not.

An AI model should never be the sole judge of its own output.

A persuasive response is not evidence. Agreement from the same underlying intelligence is not independent review. Completion must be earned through challenge, mechanical checks, and preserved evidence.

When the work is done, Sneferu delivers it. When it is not, it says what remains.

AI can generate answers. Sneferu makes the answer survive an argument.

Three ways to build.

Describe what you want and it writes the job. Fill out the form and launch it yourself. Or save it, put it on the board, and let it run while you sleep.

Run entry

One door into every production line.

Choose what you want out the other end, shape the run, choose the cast and spending limit, then read the exact request before anything runs.

Opening the page never starts or replaces a run. Nothing can launch from that state, and the button says so.
Run entry
Snef

An assistant that genuinely knows what time it is.

The same assistant answering you in the console is the one reading every handoff between models before the work is allowed to move on. Ask it what happened to a run and it answers from the records, including when something is unavailable.

Snef understands the whole system, and sees every model handoff. Your go-to to build anything without using the UI.
The assistant
Work Queue

Save a run, and the queue runs itself.

Any run can be saved as a task with its full configuration. Tasks can be reordered, queued, and left to start on their own overnight. Lessons from finished work are carried into new work.

Task queue. Easy way to turn ideas into products and systems without wasting any time.

UI Specification — Life Skills Foundations

1. Goal & Framework Reconciliation

Product

Life Skills Foundations is a printable, age-banded life-skills curriculum for homeschooling families, sold as a $25 one-time founding pilot. The product consists of four module packs (Manners, Money, Household, First Paycheck), each with dual age bands (5–8 and 9–12; Module 4 is 9–12 only), delivered as downloadable PDFs. The buyer is a homeschooling parent; the operator is a solo retired individual managing the business from a computer.

Framework Tension

The operator chose vite+react+shadcn. The backend detects as python_library — a build-time content pipeline with no HTTP routes, no server, no database, and no third-party packages. The public Python functions (build_all, render_all, all_module_band_pairs, pack_slug, render_pack_html, render_pack_pdf, etc.) are build-time tools invoked from the command line, not runtime endpoints.

This is not a contradiction. The backend is a static-site-generating content pipeline: Python code produces static files (HTML packs, PDFs, zip bundles) at build time. The React app is the presentation and operator layer that consumes the pipeline's output and replaces the scaffolded site/ directory.

Resolution

The React app attaches to the backend via a build-time data bridge, not a runtime API:

  1. What serves the app shell: A static file host (Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages, or any host that serves static files). The Vite build produces a dist/ directory containing the SPA, pre-rendered pack assets, and PDFs. No Node.js server runs in production.
  1. How the client reaches the endpoints listed above: It does not reach them at runtime. A build-time script (tools/export_curriculum.py) calls all_module_band_pairs(), pack_slug(), and reads MODULES, TOOLS, BAND_LABELS, PRODUCT_NAME, PRODUCT_SUBTITLE, PRICE_USD, GUARANTEE_DAYS from content/curriculum.py to produce src/data/curriculum.json. This JSON is imported by the React app at build time via Vite's JSON import. The Python renderers (render_all in both render_html.py and render_pdf.py) and build_all / zip_bundles are invoked from the command line before npm run build to regenerate PDFs and zip bundles. No HTTP endpoint is invented.
  1. What happens to scaffolded pages: The current site/ directory (landing page, pack HTML, assets, PDFs) is superseded entirely by the Vite build output in dist/. Specifically:
  • site/index.html → React app's / route
  • site/packs/*.html → React app's /packs/:slug routes (rendered from curriculum data in React)
  • site/packs/pdf/*.pdf → Copied to dist/packs/pdf/ during the Vite build (still Python-generated; the React app does not produce PDFs)
  • site/assets/config.js → Replaced by public/config.json (same runtime-config pattern, consumed by React)
  • site/assets/site.js → Replaced by React state and effect logic
  • site/assets/site.css → Replaced by Tailwind CSS + shadcn theme + global print styles

The site/ directory is retained in the repository as the Python pipeline's output target (pack HTML and PDFs are still generated there by tools/build.py), but it is no longer the deployed artifact. dist/ is deployed.

2. Architecture

System Diagram
content/curriculum.py  (single source of truth: MODULES, TOOLS, BAND_LABELS)
        │
        ├──► tools/build.py ──► site/packs/*.html + site/packs/pdf/*.pdf + dist/*.zip
        │
        ├──► tools/export_curriculum.py ──► src/data/curriculum.json
        │
        └──► tests/ (stdlib unittest, 48 tests)
                │
                ▼
        npm run build (Vite)
                │
                ├──► React app compiled from src/
                ├──► public/config.json copied to dist/
                ├──► site/packs/pdf/*.pdf copied to dist/packs/pdf/
                └──► dist/ (deployed static SPA)
Build Sequence

The operator runs these commands in order after editing curriculum content:

# 1. Regenerate packs, PDFs, and zip bundles from curriculum.py
python3 tools/build.py

# 2. Export curriculum data as JSON for the React app
python3 tools/export_curriculum.py

# 3. Build the React app (imports curriculum.json, copies PDFs)
npm run build

# 4. Deploy dist/ to static host
# (operator's existing host — no platform built)

For local development:

python3 tools/export_curriculum.py && npm run dev
Data Flow at Runtime (Deployed SPA)
Browser loads dist/index.html
  → React app mounts
  → Fetches /config.json (runtime config: checkoutUrl, contactEmail)
  → Imports curriculum.json (bundled at build time)
  → Renders landing page or pack preview based on route
  → PDF download links point to /packs/pdf/<slug>.pdf (static assets)
  → Buy button redirects to external checkout (Gumroad/PayPal)

No runtime API calls. No server. No database. No user accounts. No forms. No child data.

3. Data Bridge — tools/export_curriculum.py

Purpose

Export the curriculum data structures from content/curriculum.py into a JSON file that the React app imports at build time. This is the only connection between the Python backend and the React frontend.

Script Specification
"""Export curriculum data as JSON for the Vite/React frontend.

Called before `npm run build` or `npm run dev`. Reads the same
content/curriculum.py module that the Python renderers use, so the
React app and the generated PDFs always share one source of truth.

Output: src/data/curriculum.json
"""

The packs array is the flattened, route-ready form of all_module_band_pairs() with pack_slug() applied. It contains 7 entries (M1–M3 × 2 bands + M4 × 1 band).

4. TypeScript Types

All types live in src/types/curriculum.ts. They mirror the Python data structures exactly.

// src/types/curriculum.ts

export type BandKey = "5-8" | "9-12";

}

export interface ChoreTrackerTool {

export interface SavingsLogTool {

export interface RecipeCardTool {
  kind: "recipe_card";
  title: string;

export interface DoublingWorksheetTool {
  kind: "doubling_worksheet";
  title: string;

export interface CertificateTool {
  kind: "certificate";
  title: string;

export type Tool =
  | TableSettingDiagramTool
  | TemplateCardTool
  | ChoreTrackerTool
  | SavingsLogTool
  | RecipeCardTool

export type ToolMap = Record<string, Tool>;

export interface BandLabels {

  "9-12": string;
}

export interface Pack {

  moduleDomain: string;
  moduleTagline: string;

  tools: string[];
  checklist: string[];

  bandLabels: BandLabels;

  tools: ToolMap;

5. Routing Model

Router: React Router v6 (BrowserRouter).

Route Table
RouteComponentPurposeDeployed
/LandingPageMarketing landing page with buy CTAYes
/packs/:slugPackPreviewPagePrintable pack preview + PDF downloadYes
/adminAdminPageOperator dashboard (content overview, build status, config, pilot tracker)No (dev only)
*NotFoundPage404 → redirect to /Yes
Route Parameters
  • :slug — the pack slug produced by pack_slug(module, band_key), e.g., module-1-manners-ages-5-8. The PackPreviewPage looks up the pack in curriculumData.packs by slug. If not found, renders NotFoundPage.
Navigation
  • The landing page's header nav uses anchor links to in-page sections (#inside, #how, #sample, #faq, #buy) via react-router's useNavigate with hash, or standard <a href="#..."> for same-page scroll.
  • Sample page links use <Link to="/packs/module-1-manners-ages-5-8">.
  • The admin route is accessible only in development (guarded by an environment check: import.meta.env.DEV). In production builds, navigating to /admin redirects to /.

6. Runtime Configuration

File: public/config.json
{
  "checkoutUrl": "",
  "contactEmail": "pilot@example.com"
}

This file is copied verbatim to dist/config.json by the Vite build. The operator edits it post-build to set the checkout URL — same pattern as the current site/assets/config.js, but JSON instead of JS.

Loading
// src/config/runtime-config.ts

import type { RuntimeConfig } from "@/types/curriculum";

let cachedConfig: RuntimeConfig | null = null;

export async function loadConfig(): Promise<RuntimeConfig> {
  if (cachedConfig) return cachedConfig;
  const res = await fetch("/config.json");
  if (!res.ok) {
    return { checkoutUrl: "", contactEmail: "" };
  }
  cachedConfig = await res.json();
  return cachedConfig;
}

export function isCheckoutReady(url: string): boolean {
  return /^https:\/\//i.test(url.trim());
}
Honest Checkout Pattern

The BuySection component checks isCheckoutReady(config.checkoutUrl):

  • If true: the buy button is an <a href={config.checkoutUrl} rel="noopener"> that opens the external checkout.
  • If false: the buy button shows the text "Opens at launch" and reveals a note: "Checkout link opens when the pilot launches — email {contactEmail} to be notified."

This preserves the existing product contract: no fake checkout, ever.

9. Print Contract

Global Print Styles (src/styles/print.css)
@media print {
  /* Hide all screen-only chrome */
  .print-hide {
    display: none !important;
  }

  /* Reset page geometry */
  @page {
    size: Letter;
    margin: 0.75in;
  }

  /* Pack content uses these */
  .sheet {
    page-break-before: always;
  }

  .sheet:first-of-type {
    page-break-before: avoid;
  }

  /* Ensure black text on white */
  body {
    color: #000 !important;
    background: #fff !important;
    font-size: 11pt;
    line-height: 1.45;
  }

  /* Remove sticky positioning */
  header, .sticky {
    position: static !important;
  }
}
Pack Page Print Behavior

The PrintLayout component wraps the pack content:

  • Screen header (back button, print button, PDF download) has class print-hide
  • Each major section (cover, parent guide, each lesson, each tool, checklist) is wrapped in a <div className="sheet">
  • The first sheet has page-break-before: avoid to prevent a blank first page
  • All visual elements (SVG diagrams, table borders, checkboxes) use black strokes/fills only — no color dependencies
  • Font family: Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif (matches current pack HTML)
  • The window.print() call is triggered by the "Print this pack" button
PDF vs Browser Print

The "Download PDF" button links to the Python-generated PDF at pack.pdfPath (e.g., /packs/pdf/module-1-manners-ages-5-8.pdf). This is the authoritative customer deliverable — generated by the custom stdlib PDF writer in tools/pdfgen.py, verified by the test suite. The browser print option is a convenience for previewing; the PDF is the canonical artifact.

10. State Management

Customer-Facing Pages

No complex state management needed. State is minimal:

  • Route state: React Router handles URL → component mapping
  • Config state: Loaded once via loadConfig(), stored in a React context (ConfigContext)
  • FAQ accordion state: Local component state via shadcn Accordion
  • No form state: There are no forms on customer-facing pages (COPPA compliance)
  • No cart state: Checkout is external (Gumroad/PayPal)
Admin Dashboard
  • Active tab: Local state in AdminPage
  • Content tree expansion: Local state in ContentTree
  • Checkout config form: Local state in CheckoutConfigForm, saved via dev-server middleware
  • Pilot tracking data: localStorage with keys:
  • lsf_pilot_sales — JSON array of { date: string, count: number, notes: string }
  • lsf_pilot_reports — JSON array of { date: string, count: number, notes: string }
Config Context
// src/config/ConfigContext.tsx

import { createContext, useContext, useEffect, useState } from "react";
import type { RuntimeConfig } from "@/types/curriculum";
import { loadConfig } from "@/config/runtime-config";

const ConfigContext = createContext<RuntimeConfig | null>(null);

export function ConfigProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [config, setConfig] = useState<RuntimeConfig | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    loadConfig().then(setConfig);
  }, []);

  if (!config) return null; // or a loading skeleton
  return (
    <ConfigContext.Provider value={config}>
      {children}
    </ConfigContext.Provider>
  );
}

export function useConfig() {
  const config = useContext(ConfigContext);
  if (!config) throw new Error("useConfig must be used within ConfigProvider");
  return config;
}

11. Vite Configuration

vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import path from "path";
import { copyFileSync, mkdirSync, readdirSync } from "fs";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    react(),
    {
      name: "copy-pdfs",
      closeBundle() {
        const srcDir = path.resolve(__dirname, "site/packs/pdf");
        const destDir = path.resolve(__dirname, "dist/packs/pdf");
        mkdirSync(destDir, { recursive: true });
        for (const file of readdirSync(srcDir)) {
          if (file.endsWith(".pdf")) {
            copyFileSync(path.join(srcDir, file), path.join(destDir, file));
          }
        }
      },
    },
    {
      name: "admin-dev-bridge",
      apply: "serve", // dev only
      configureServer(server) {
        server.middlewares.use(async (req, res, next) => {
          if (req.url === "/api/save-config" && req.method === "POST") {
            // Read body, write to public/config.json
            // This is a dev-only convenience, not a production endpoint
            let body = "";
            req.on("data", chunk => body += chunk);
            req.on("end", () => {
              const config = JSON.parse(body);
              const fs = await import("fs");
              fs.writeFileSync(
                path.resolve(__dirname, "public/config.json"),
                JSON.stringify(config, null, 2)
              );
              res.setHeader("Content-Type", "application/json");
              res.end(JSON.stringify({ ok: true }));
            });
          } else {
            next();
          }
        });
      },
    },
  ],
  resolve: {
    alias: {
      "@": path.resolve(__dirname, "./src"),
    },
  },
  build: {
    outDir: "dist",
    emptyOutDir: true,
  },
});

13. tools/export_curriculum.py — Implementation Specification

"""Export curriculum data as JSON for the Vite/React frontend.

Called before `npm run build` or `npm run dev`. Reads the same
content/curriculum.py module that the Python renderers use.

Output: src/data/curriculum.json

This script does NOT invent endpoints — it reads existing public
data structures (MODULES, TOOLS, BAND_LABELS, PRODUCT_NAME,
PRODUCT_SUBTITLE, PRICE_USD, GUARANTEE_DAYS) and calls existing
public functions (all_module_band_pairs, pack_slug).
"""

import json
import os
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))

from content.curriculum import (
    MODULES, TOOLS, BAND_LABELS, PRODUCT_NAME, PRODUCT_SUBTITLE,
    PRICE_USD, GUARANTEE_DAYS, all_module_band_pairs, pack_slug,
)

REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
OUT_PATH = os.path.join(REPO_ROOT, "src", "data", "curriculum.json")


def export():
    packs = []
    for module, band_key, band in all_module_band_pairs():
        slug = pack_slug(module, band_key)
        packs.append({
            "slug": slug,
            "moduleId": module["id"],
            "bandKey": band_key,
            "bandLabel": BAND_LABELS[band_key],
            "moduleNumber": module["number"],
            "moduleTitle": module["title"],
            "moduleDomain": module["domain"],
            "moduleTagline": module["tagline"],
            "parentIntro": module["parent_intro"],
            "lessons": band["lessons"],
            "tools": band["tools"],
            "checklist": band["checklist"],
            "pdfPath": "/packs/pdf/%s.pdf" % slug,
        })

    data = {
        "product": {
            "name": PRODUCT_NAME,
            "subtitle": PRODUCT_SUBTITLE,
            "priceUsd": PRICE_USD,
            "guaranteeDays": GUARANTEE_DAYS,
        },
        "bandLabels": BAND_LABELS,
        "modules": MODULES,
        "tools": TOOLS,
        "packs": packs,
        "exportedAt": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    }

    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(OUT_PATH), exist_ok=True)
    with open(OUT_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        json.dump(data, fh, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

    print("Exported curriculum data to %s (%d packs)" % (OUT_PATH, len(packs)))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    export()

Note on ASCII constraint: content/curriculum.py uses plain ASCII only (the stdlib PDF renderer requires Latin-1). The JSON export preserves this — all curriculum text is ASCII. The HTML entities (&ldquo;, &rdquo;, &#x27;) that the Python HTML renderer applies at render time are NOT present in the JSON; the React app handles typographic rendering via CSS or manual entity insertion in components.

14. Compliance & Safety Constraints

These constraints are carried forward from the product contract and must be enforced in the UI:

COPPA — No Child Data
  • No forms on any customer-facing page. The landing page has no inputs, no textareas, no selects.
  • The admin checkout config form is operator-facing and dev-only — it never appears in production.
  • The pilot tracker uses localStorage only — no data is transmitted anywhere.
  • The FAQ explicitly states: "We never collect any information from children."
  • The footer states: "We never collect information from children."
Module 4 — Concepts Only
  • The admin OverviewPanel runs a client-side compliance check: scans all Module 4 text (lessons, say, demonstrate, practice, checklist) for banned terms: stock, invest, portfolio, ticker, broker, market, crypto, dividend, 401k, ira, etf, mutual fund, bond
  • If any banned term is found, a destructive badge is shown
  • The PackPreviewPage for Module 4 renders the concepts-only disclaimer from the curriculum data (the parent_intro contains "no investment recommendations, no market predictions, and no product suggestions of any kind")
Honest Checkout — No Fake Checkout
  • The BuySection component uses isCheckoutReady() to check if checkoutUrl is a valid https:// URL
  • If not ready, the button shows "Opens at launch" and reveals a notification note
  • If ready, the button is a plain <a> link to the external checkout with rel="noopener"
  • No checkout is ever simulated, faked, or proxied
No External Dependencies in Pack Print Output
  • Pack preview pages use inline SVG for diagrams (no external image references)
  • Print CSS is bundled (no external stylesheet references in print mode)
  • All pack content renders from curriculum.json — no runtime fetches when viewing a pack
No Third-Party Copyrighted Material
  • All curriculum text comes from content/curriculum.py (operator-authored, original)
  • No stock images, no external fonts, no third-party CSS frameworks in pack print output
  • The landing page uses shadcn/ui components and Tailwind CSS — both are open-source, not copyrighted assets

15. Staleness Detection

Build-Time Staleness

The existing Python test suite (tests/test_render.py) includes a staleness test that checks committed pack HTML files against a fresh render. This remains unchanged — it runs via python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t ..

React App Staleness

The curriculum.json file includes an exportedAt timestamp. The admin BuildPanel displays this timestamp and shows an Alert if:

  • The timestamp is more than 1 hour old (informational — "Last export was more than 1 hour ago. Re-run python3 tools/export_curriculum.py if you've edited curriculum content.")
  • This is a soft check — the admin panel cannot read the filesystem to compare against curriculum.py's modification time from the browser
Manual Rebuild Reminder

The admin BuildPanel always shows the rebuild command sequence:

python3 tools/build.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .
python3 tools/export_curriculum.py
npm run build

16. Deployment

Deployed Artifact

The dist/ directory produced by npm run build is the deployed artifact. It contains:

dist/
  index.html                    — SPA entry point
  config.json                   — Runtime config (operator edits post-build)
  assets/
    *.js                        — Bundled JavaScript
    *.css                       — Bundled CSS (Tailwind + shadcn + print)
  packs/
    pdf/
      module-1-manners-ages-5-8.pdf
      module-1-manners-ages-9-12.pdf
      module-2-money-ages-5-8.pdf
      module-2-money-ages-9-12.pdf
      module-3-household-ages-5-8.pdf
      module-3-household-ages-9-12.pdf
      module-4-first-paycheck-ages-9-12.pdf
Static Hosting

The SPA uses BrowserRouter, which requires the host to redirect all routes to index.html (standard SPA hosting). Configure the host's redirect rules:

  • Netlify: _redirects file with /* /index.html 200
  • Vercel: vercel.json with rewrites
  • GitHub Pages: 404.html fallback or HashRouter alternative
  • Any static host: fallback to index.html for unknown paths
Post-Build Config Edit

After deploying, the operator edits dist/config.json (or public/config.json before building) to set the checkout URL:

{
  "checkoutUrl": "https://gumroad.com/l/your-product-id",
  "contactEmail": "operator@example.com"
}

No rebuild is needed to change the checkout URL — just edit the JSON file on the host.

Scaffolded FileReplacementMechanism
site/index.htmlLandingPage at route /React component rendered by Vite, output to dist/index.html
site/packs/*.html (7 files)PackPreviewPage at route /packs/:slug (7 slugs)React components rendered from curriculum.json data

The site/ directory remains in the repository as the Python pipeline's output target. tools/build.py still writes packs and PDFs there. The Vite build copies the PDFs to dist/. The site/packs/*.html files become unnecessary for deployment but remain as Python-generated artifacts for testing and as a fallback.

18. Accessibility

  • All interactive elements are keyboard navigable (shadcn components handle this by default)
  • SVG diagrams include role="img" and aria-label attributes
  • Print buttons and download links have descriptive text labels
  • Color contrast: the warm-paper theme (#1d1a16 on #faf7f2) meets WCAG AA for normal text
  • No color-only differentiation: all visual distinctions (borders, bold text, layout) work in black-and-white print
  • FAQ accordion uses semantic buttons with ARIA attributes (shadcn Accordion provides this)

19. Known Limitations (Honest)

  1. No runtime content editing. Content is edited in content/curriculum.py and rebuilt. The admin dashboard is read-only for content. This is by design — the product contract forbids building a platform.
  1. Pilot tracking is manual. No analytics, no tracking pixels, no webhook from Gumroad/PayPal. The operator enters sales counts by hand. This is by design — no custom platform or automated integration is built.
  1. PDFs remain Python-generated. The React app does not produce PDFs. The custom stdlib PDF writer in tools/pdfgen.py is the authoritative PDF generator, verified by the test suite. The React app's "Print this pack" button uses the browser's print dialog, which is a convenience preview, not the canonical artifact.
  1. Staleness detection is soft. The admin panel shows the last export timestamp but cannot automatically detect if curriculum.py has been edited since. The operator must follow the rebuild sequence manually.
  1. Pack print fidelity depends on browser. The browser's print rendering may differ slightly from the Python-generated PDF (font metrics, page break positions). The PDF download is the authoritative deliverable; browser print is a convenience.
  1. Admin is dev-only. The /admin route is guarded by import.meta.env.DEV. In production builds, the admin code is included in the bundle (tree-shaking does not remove it because it's a route component), but the route redirects to /. A more thorough approach would use environment-specific entry points, but that adds build complexity disproportionate to the value for a solo operator.

20. Obligation Responses

Framework reconciliation (vite+react+shadcn vs python_library): Resolved in Section 1. The React app is a static SPA that attaches to the Python backend via a build-time JSON export. No HTTP endpoints are invented. The app shell is served by a static file host. The scaffolded site/ pages are superseded by Vite's dist/ output.

Every screen reachable through listed entry points: The landing page and pack previews consume data from curriculum.json, which is produced by calling all_module_band_pairs(), pack_slug(), and reading MODULES, TOOLS, BAND_LABELS, PRODUCT_NAME, PRODUCT_SUBTITLE, PRICE_USD, GUARANTEE_DAYS — all public Python functions/classes listed in the manifest. The admin dashboard displays the same data in read-only form. PDF download links point to files generated by render_all() and build_all(). No endpoint outside the manifest is used.

Product contract preserved: $25 one-time price, 7-day guarantee, external checkout (Gumroad/PayPal), no custom platform, no user accounts, no child data, no forms, Module 4 concepts-only, no investment advice, all materials original, US Letter black-and-white printable, supplemental enrichment positioning. All carried forward.

The finished specificationafter four turns through the system

Life Skills Foundations — Pilot Deck UI Specification

Artifact: canonical ui_spec, merged revision (synthesis of independent revisions)
Product under contract: Life Skills Foundations founding pilot — four printable, age-banded life-skills module packs, $25 one-time, sold through an external hosted checkout to 40 homeschooling families in eight weeks Interface stack (operator decision, binding): Vite + React + TypeScript + shadcn/ui
Backend under contract: the stdlib Python content pipeline exactly as enumerated in the Backend Artifact Manifest — content/curriculum.py, tools/render_html.py, tools/render_pdf.py, tools/pdfgen.py, tools/build.py, and the tests/ suite. No HTTP routes exist in the product; none are added. The routes defined in §7 of this spec are the design contract for a new tools/console.py bridge file that the implementer must create; they do not exist in any current server and are not modifications to orchestrator/api/server.py or any other existing file. §7.1's function-signature and constant-name verification is the gate against hallucination — the implementer verifies every call against the actual source before the endpoint ships.

1. Purpose and Product Frame

The curriculum product is finished and verified: seven self-contained pack HTML files, seven US-Letter PDFs, five customer zip bundles, a static landing page, and 48 passing stdlib tests. What is missing is any humane way for the operator to run it. Today every operational act is a terminal command or a hand-edited file, and the single most important business artifact — the eight-week, 40-family pilot experiment with explicit kill criteria (B10 experiments E-001 through E-004) — has no tooling whatsoever.

This specification defines Pilot Deck: a single-user, locally served web console that gathers the entire operate loop — inspect the curriculum, preview the deliverables, rebuild, re-validate, package, check launch readiness, configure checkout, and track the pilot against its thresholds — into one browser window. The operator opens a terminal exactly once to start the console; after that, every routine action is a button, a form, or a visual status display.

Pilot Deck is operator tooling. It is not the product, not a storefront, not a CMS, and not a customer surface of any kind. It never collects data from children, never processes payments, and never replaces the static customer-facing site.

Architectural foundation of this revision: the bridge never imports product Python modules in its own process. Every operation that touches product code spawns a fresh Python subprocess that imports the modules in a clean interpreter, calls the manifest-listed function, serializes the result to JSON on stdout, and exits. There is no importlib.reload, no redirect_stdout in server threads, no in-process module state of any kind. This single decision eliminates the reload-safety, CSRF-via-GET-side-effects, stdout thread-unsafety, and stale-module-state failure classes by construction.

Cross-platform commitment: the operator is a retired, not-very-mobile individual who may use a Windows laptop. Every subprocess management mechanism in this spec uses the cross-platform subprocess.Popen API (.terminate(), .kill()) rather than Unix-exclusive signals. The bridge and wrapper are stdlib-only and must run on any platform that supports Python 3.8+. The subprocess executable is always sys.executable (the interpreter running the bridge), never a hardcoded 'python3' string that may not exist on PATH under Windows.

2. Framework Reconciliation

The operator chose vite+react+shadcn. That decision is an input to this design, not a topic for debate. The candidate as built detects as python_library because its true surface is a set of importable Python functions plus generated files on disk — the manifest itself notes the UI "may need to be a CLI dashboard, library demo, or batch interface." These facts are not in conflict; they determine the attachment model.

Reconciliation, stated as binding decisions:

AspectDecisionRationale
Customer-facing siteRemains static, Python-generated, untouched. site/index.html, site/assets/, site/packs/.html, site/packs/pdf/*.pdf are deliverables, not scaffolding.Product contract forbids a custom storefront. Pack pages carry test-pinned print contracts (US Letter, B&W-safe, zero external references). Rebuilding in React would display content the test suite never validated and insert an npm build between the operator and a deliverable that regenerates with one stdlib command.
Operator consoleSeparate Vite + React + TS + shadcn/ui SPA in a new console/ directory. Never shipped to customers, never referenced by site/ output.Additive and fully reversible. If console/ is deleted, python3 tools/build.py and the test suite work byte-identically.
Attachment mechanismTwo new stdlib-only Python files. tools/console.py: a thin http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer that binds 127.0.0.1 only (default port 8787, --port to override), serves compiled assets from console/dist/, serves /site/ and /artifacts/ as read-only static files for local preview, and dispatches /api/* routes. tools/console_bridge.py: a subprocess wrapper that imports product modules, calls manifest-listed functions, and emits JSON on stdout.Extends the project's existing serving idiom (packaging.json already declares python3 -m http.server --directory site as the runtime test server). No second runtime, no Flask or FastAPI (worktree rules forbid third-party installs), no Node-based server. A dedicated wrapper file — rather than ad-hoc python3 -c one-liners — avoids shell-quoting hazards and is independently testable.
How the client reaches manifest entry pointsEach /api/* route that needs product data spawns [sys.executable, 'tools/console_bridge.py', '<command>', ...args] via subprocess.Popen with stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE, text=True, cwd=<repo root>, and a per-operation timeout enforced by proc.communicate(timeout=<limit>) (§6.8). The wrapper imports the relevant module fresh, calls the function, prints structured JSON, and exits. Routes that serve committed bytes (pack HTML/PDF), config, pilot state, or packaging metadata are pure file I/O handled directly by the bridge — no subprocess needed because no product module is imported.Fresh process per call = fresh imports = nothing to reload. sys.executable guarantees the same interpreter runs the wrapper, satisfying the cross-platform commitment. Structured JSON preserves type fidelity. The communicate(timeout=…) API provides cross-platform timeout and kill capability. The trade-off is roughly 0.1–0.5s latency per API call, acceptable for a single-user local tool with TanStack Query caching.
Dev vs. production servingDev: python3 tools/console.py --dev plus npm run dev in console/ (Vite on 5173) with proxy to bridge (8787), using changeOrigin: true so the proxy rewrites the Host header to 127.0.0.1:8787 before forwarding. Production: one-time npm run build produces console/dist/; then python3 tools/console.py serves everything. Operator opens http://127.0.0.1:8787.Single-command production start for a non-technical operator. Two-terminal dev flow only for the implementer. changeOrigin: true is mandatory: without it, the browser's Host: localhost:5173 header is forwarded to the bridge, which rejects it with 403 because the Host guard only accepts 127.0.0.1:{port} and localhost:{port} on the bridge's own port. With changeOrigin, the Host guard passes unmodified. The --dev flag widens only the Origin allowlist (§6.2); the Host allowlist never changes.
Third-party Python packagesNone. Bridge and wrapper use only stdlib: http.server, json, os, sys, subprocess, threading, pathlib, re, argparse, tempfile, unittest, io, contextlib, time, urllib.parse, html.Preserves the product's zero-dependency posture. node_modules/ stays in console/ and is gitignored; it never ships to customers.
Bridge serves customer site locallyYes, for local preview only. GET /site/ serves files from site/ so the operator can preview the customer landing page and pack pages in-app without a second server process. GET /artifacts/ serves customer zip bundles from the project-root dist/ directory for operator download. Both are read-only, path-confined (§6.6), and never deployed. The deployed customer site remains on its external static host. When the console is not running, python3 -m http.server --directory site serves the product identically to before.Reconciles the author-seat disagreement: the "customer site not served by bridge" position was about deployment; local preview serving is a convenience, not a deployment. The route prefix /artifacts/ (not /dist/) is used deliberately to eliminate the naming collision between the project-root dist/ (zip bundles) and console/dist/ (Vite build output).

3. What the Console Replaces — and What It Must Never Touch

The brief asks what happens to the scaffolded pages. The answer is sharp and this spec commits to it.

Customer-facing files are deliverables, not scaffolding. site/index.html carries the $25 price, 7-day guarantee, compliance FAQ, and honest-checkout behavior that tests pin. The seven site/packs/*.html files are validated byte-for-byte against fresh renders (tests/test_render.py). The print contract (@page Letter, no external references, black-and-white safe) is test-enforced on the Python renderers. Rebuilding any of this in React would (a) drift toward the "no custom storefront" prohibition, (b) display pack content the test suite never validated, and (c) insert an npm build between the operator and a deliverable that currently regenerates with one stdlib command. They remain static, Python-generated, and untouched. Pilot Deck previews the committed bytes; it never re-renders pack content from curriculum data in React.

What the console replaces is the scaffolding of the operator's own workflow:

Manual act todayReplaced by
python3 tools/build.pyBuild screen, one button, live log
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .Checks screen, one button, structured results with pass/fail detail
python3 -m http.server … --directory site plus tab-hopping to previewIn-app preview of every committed pack, PDF, and the landing page
Reading freshness failures out of test scrollbackPer-pack Fresh / Stale / Missing badges, visible before anything breaks
Hand-editing site/assets/config.jsLaunch screen with a validated two-field form (the console's only write to product files)
Sales tracked on paper or nowherePilot screen: per-channel entry, threshold banners, report tally

4. The Operator and the Constraints That Shape the Design

One user: a solo, retired operator (B0), self-described as not very mobile, strong on the phone and with people, diligent with processes, not a developer, working roughly 20 hours per week, wanting the business runnable "from my computer, as automated as possible." Design consequences that bind every screen:

  1. No terminal exposure after initial startup. The operator runs python3 tools/console.py once, then works in the browser. Where a contract-bound manual step genuinely exists (editing lesson text in content/curriculum.py, uploading zips to a file host, creating the Gumroad listing), the console shows the exact file path, the exact action, and then gets out of the way. It never pretends a manual step is automatic.
  1. Legibility over density. Base UI text 14px or larger. Generous hit targets (minimum 40×40px). One primary action per screen, pinned top-right or in a dedicated action bar. Every status rendered as icon-plus-words — never color alone. This mirrors the product's own black-and-white print contract and is simply good accessibility for a retired user.
  1. No destructive actions against product files. The two consequential actions (Build, Run checks) are idempotent and safe to repeat. There is no delete, no reset, no overwrite of source data or customer deliverables. The only product-file mutation is site/assets/config.js, a two-field, validated, deterministically regenerable write (§7.4). Pilot state — sales, feedback, acceptance checklist, kill acknowledgments — can be reset with double confirmation via a dedicated POST /api/pilot/reset endpoint (§7.3) that bypasses the optimistic-concurrency guard; this clears console/data/pilot-state.json to defaults and nothing else. It never touches product files, and never touches build/test history, which is stored separately in console/data/console-state.json.
  1. The experiment is the headline. The pilot exists to answer "will 40 households pay $25 in eight weeks?" with kill thresholds attached (B10: E-001 community, kill <5 in 14 days; E-002 through E-004 with their own thresholds). The console treats those numbers as first-class interface, not as buried documentation. Kill-threshold breaches require explicit operator acknowledgment (§10.7) — the console is an active experiment guard, not a passive display, and the operator's walk-away gates are binding.
  1. Accessibility is binding, not aspirational. Every iframe carries a title attribute. Every icon-only button carries aria-label. A skip-to-main-content link is the first focusable element on every screen, visible on first Tab press. Focus indicators are visible (2px ring, 2px offset) on all interactive elements and are never removed. Heading hierarchy is one h1 per page, h2 per section, h3 per card, with no skipped levels. Loading containers use aria-busy; status changes are announced via aria-live="polite" regions.
  1. Cross-platform operation is binding. The operator may use Windows. Subprocess management uses Popen.terminate() (SIGTERM on Unix, TerminateProcess on Windows) and Popen.kill() (SIGKILL on Unix, TerminateProcess on Windows) — never raw os.kill with signal.SIGTERM. The subprocess executable is sys.executable, not a hardcoded 'python3'. File paths use os.path.join throughout. No platform-specific assumptions about signal behavior, file locking, or process semantics.

5. Positions Taken Where the Drafts Disagreed

Seven author drafts reached genuinely different conclusions. This spec takes a side on each and states the rationale.

5.1 Should the React app absorb the customer landing page and pack pages?
Rejected. The product contract forbids building a storefront; the pack pages are test-pinned deliverables; the buyer arrives from a Facebook group and needs a fast static page, not a client-side bundle. The console previews and verifies the customer surface; it does not become it. All author seats agreed.

5.2 What language is the bridge, and what is its execution model?
Stdlib Python, and subprocess-per-call. Flask (a third-party package) is forbidden by worktree rules. A Node helper (a second runtime on a non-technical operator's machine, with structured Python data flattened through stdout) is rejected. importlib.reload on every API call — the original spec's approach — is rejected: it is a CSRF vector on GET requests (side effects in GET handlers), thread-unsafe with redirect_stdout under ThreadingHTTPServer, and fragile for modules not written with hot-reloading in mind. The majority "restart required" position is achieved in a strictly better form: every request that needs product data gets a fresh subprocess with a clean interpreter, so there is nothing to reload and nothing to restart. Build and test also run as subprocesses with server-side timeouts and a build lock. Subprocess termination uses the cross-platform Popen API (§6.8). The subprocess executable is sys.executable, not 'python3', satisfying the Windows cross-platform commitment.

5.3 Does the console edit curriculum content?
Rejected, firmly. content/curriculum.py is executable Python under a test-pinned contract (ASCII-only content, banned-term lists for Module 4, schema enforced by _lesson()). A web form that serializes Python source is a corruption machine. Content editing stays in the operator's text editor; the console shows exactly where to edit, and the next subprocess call re-reads from disk automatically.

5.4 Does the console write anything at all?
One product file, two operator-local files. The product-file write is site/assets/config.js via PUT /api/config, because the launch checklist's critical step — pasting the hosted-checkout URL — is precisely where a non-technical operator will produce a syntax error. The file is four lines, documented as an operator knob (OPERATOR_GUIDE.md step 1), and deterministically regenerable from two validated strings (§7.4). The Launch screen carries a persistent warning that saving via the form replaces the entire file and that hand-edits will be overwritten. The operator-local writes are console/data/pilot-state.json (pilot tracking) and console/data/console-state.json (build/test history). Neither is a product file; neither is deployed; both are gitignored.

5.5 Where does sales data come from, and where is it persisted?
Manual entry, persisted server-side via the bridge with optimistic concurrency control. Gumroad API integration is rejected for the pilot: forty sales over eight weeks is countable from checkout receipt emails, and an API integration means stored credentials (the risk register already flags account compromise), network egress, and failure modes the operator cannot debug. Persistence is console/data/pilot-state.json via GET/PUT /api/pilot — not browser localStorage, which is cleared by cache wipes, cannot be exported from the bridge, and previously created an internal contradiction in this spec. localStorage is used only for UI conveniences (launch-checklist checkboxes, sidebar collapsed state), never for pilot data.

Concurrency control on pilot saves: the pilot state file includes a _version integer managed by the bridge and incremented on each successful write. PUT /api/pilot must include the _version the client received from its last GET. If the stored version does not match, the bridge returns HTTP 409 with { ok: false, error: "Pilot data was modified in another session. The latest version has been loaded.", type: "pilot_version_conflict", data: <current state> } — the current state rides the 409 response so the client does not need a second round-trip to display it. The client opens a VersionConflictDialog prompting the operator to review the latest state and re-enter their changes (§7.5, §10.7). An integer counter is used rather than a timestamp: integer comparison is exact, immune to clock granularity and same-second collisions, and trivially testable. This prevents silent data loss when the operator has two tabs open or refreshes one tab while another holds stale state.

Pilot reset bypasses the concurrency guard. The POST /api/pilot/reset endpoint (§7.3) writes the default object with _version: 0 without checking the stored version. This is necessary because the stored version will almost always be greater than 0 after any pilot activity, so a PUT /api/pilot with _version: 0 would always be rejected as a version conflict — making a PUT-based reset action dead code. The concurrency guard exists to prevent accidental data loss from stale tabs; reset is an intentional, double-confirmed operator act that must not be blocked by the very guard designed to prevent accidental loss. The reset endpoint is called only after the typed-RESET confirmation in the UI (§10.7), preserving the deliberate-safeguard posture while making the action actually work.

5.6 Where does the console run?
Loopback only. An unauthenticated operator console with build and test capability must never be internet-reachable. The bridge binds 127.0.0.1, refuses any other bind at startup, enforces an exact-match Host-header guard on every request against a fixed two-value allowlist, and checks the Origin header (§6.2). The Host allowlist is identical in dev and production; in development the Vite proxy's mandatory changeOrigin: true rewrites the Host header before forwarding, so dev-mode calls pass the guard without widening it. The --dev flag widens only the Origin allowlist.

5.7 Routing mode: hash or browser?
BrowserRouter with bridge-side SPA fallback. The bridge controls serving in all modes, so server-side fallback is trivial; hash routing adds URL complexity for no benefit. Concrete fallback rules are specified in §6.5.

5.8 Does the bridge serve the customer site?
Yes, for local preview only, per the §2 reconciliation. /site/ and /artifacts/ are read-only, path-confined routes. The bridge never deploys anything.

5.9 Build pipeline modification: add build-manifest.json or leave untouched?
No modification to tools/build.py, and no build manifest anywhere. The majority of author seats rejected pipeline modification, and placing a manifest under site/assets/ would expose build metadata on the deployed customer site. Freshness is computed solely from filesystem mtime comparison (§6.7) — one canonical method, no secondary signals. The earlier manifest-based and byte-comparison approaches are removed.

5.10 Partial build endpoints?
Removed. POST /api/build/html and POST /api/build/pdf are not provided. The product contract requires both HTML and PDF for every pack; partial builds create a state where one format is fresh and the other stale, which confuses freshness reporting. The console exposes only POST /api/build (full build) and POST /api/test. An implementer who needs a granular rebuild during debugging uses the terminal directly.

5.11 State management library.
TanStack Query for server state; React useState for client state. No Zustand, no Redux, no React Context for global state. Client-only state is minimal and screen-local (§12).

5.12 Freshness detection scope: curriculum.py only, or all source files?
All source files. Comparing only content/curriculum.py's mtime against pack output mtimes misses edits to tools/render_html.py, tools/render_pdf.py, tools/pdfgen.py, and tools/build.py — any of which can change build output without touching curriculum.py, producing artifacts that are stale relative to the toolchain yet reported as Fresh. The freshness logic (§6.7) takes the maximum mtime across all five source files as the comparison baseline. This is a material correctness requirement, not a refinement.

5.13 Live-preview error handling: raw JSON in iframes or legible HTML?
Legible HTML error pages, for every live-render route. Live-render routes (?src=live) are loaded as iframe src attributes. If the subprocess fails (curriculum syntax error, render exception), returning a JSON error envelope causes the iframe to display raw JSON — confusing and unactionable. The bridge instead returns an HTML error page with Content-Type: text/html and HTTP 200 when any live-render subprocess fails — pack HTML, pack PDF, and tool preview alike — so the iframe renders a readable, styled error message in place. An iframe is a browsing context: it renders text/html responses regardless of what content type the app "expected," so no client-side fetch-and-inspect machinery is needed for the PDF route. The page includes the error text HTML-escaped via Python's html.escape() from the standard library (§7.2a) and a pointer to the likely cause.

5.14 Build failure response: error-only or include partial artifacts?
Include best-effort partial artifacts. A build may partially succeed (some packs rendered before an exception). The build response uses the success envelope { ok: true, data: BuildResult } where BuildResult.ok is false on build failure but BuildResult.artifacts and BuildResult.zips contain a best-effort filesystem snapshot of whatever exists on disk, gathered by os.stat() after the subprocess exits. Only timeout, lock contention, and source errors use the standard error envelope { ok: false, error, type }. This ensures the UI can always display a partial artifact table.

6.2 Bridge rules (all binding)

The bridge (tools/console.py) is a thin static file server and subprocess dispatcher. It never imports product modules.

  • Bind 127.0.0.1 only. At startup, refuse to run if asked to bind anything else. Reject any request whose Host header is not exactly 127.0.0.1:{port} or localhost:{port} with HTTP 403. The check is exact set membership against a fixed allowlist — {"127.0.0.1:" + str(port), "localhost:" + str(port)} — not substring, not regex, not a blocklist of known-bad values. Host: localhost.evil.com:8787, Host: 127.0.0.1.nip.io:8787, Host: 127.0.0.1:8788 (wrong port), and Host: [::1]:8787 must all be rejected. This allowlist never changes between dev and production. In development the Vite proxy's changeOrigin: true (§6.9) rewrites the Host header to 127.0.0.1:8787 before forwarding, so dev-mode API calls pass the guard without widening it; Host: localhost:5173 arriving directly at the bridge is rejected in every mode.
  • Origin-header check (CSRF defense). On every request, if an Origin header is present it must be exactly one of http://127.0.0.1:{port}, http://localhost:{port}, or — when the bridge was started with --dev (or LSF_CONSOLE_DEV=1) — http://localhost:5173 or http://127.0.0.1:5173 (the Vite dev server's origin, which the browser sends when the page is served from 5173 and the proxy forwards API calls to 8787; changeOrigin rewrites Host but not Origin). A present-but-unmatched Origin returns HTTP 403. The check is exact set membership — not substring, not prefix, not a blocklist. Origin: https://evil.com, Origin: null, Origin: http://localhost.evil.com, and Origin: http://127.0.0.1.evil.com must all be rejected. In production mode (no --dev), Origin: http://localhost:5173 is rejected like any other non-allowlisted origin. Requests without an Origin header (same-origin navigations, curl without explicit Origin) are allowed, because GET endpoints have no side effects under the subprocess model and the Host-header guard already restricts access to loopback — the CSRF surface is eliminated by construction, with this check as defense-in-depth.
  • No CORS headers (the app is same-origin in both dev and served modes), no cookies, no auth, no telemetry, no outbound network calls. Single local user, consistent with the product's no-accounts posture.
  • Cache-Control: no-store on every /api response and on pack/PDF/artifact bytes, because builds mutate them.
  • Subprocess execution model. All product-module calls execute via subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, 'tools/console_bridge.py', '<command>', ...args], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, cwd=<repo root>) with proc.communicate(timeout=<limit>) (§6.8). sys.executable is mandatory, not 'python3': on Windows the executable may be python or py, and sys.executable guarantees the same interpreter. No importlib.reload exists anywhere in the bridge or wrapper. Stdout/stderr are captured in the subprocess (PIPE on the Popen, and contextlib.redirect_stdout into a StringIO inside the wrapper process for build/test); no server thread ever replaces global sys.stdout, so ThreadingHTTPServer can serve status checks while a build runs.
  • Subprocess failure handling. If a subprocess exits non-zero (e.g., SyntaxError, IndentationError, NameError, or any other exception in curriculum.py), the bridge captures stderr and returns { ok: false, error: "Curriculum source error: <stderr excerpt>", type: "source_error" }. The console displays a red Alert on the affected screen: "Curriculum source has an error. Fix content/curriculum.py and try again. Error: <message>." Screens that do not depend on curriculum data (Pilot, Launch) remain usable. For iframe-facing routes (live-render pack HTML, live-render pack PDF, tool preview — routes whose response is loaded directly as an iframe src), subprocess failures return HTTP 200 with Content-Type: text/html and the HTML error page (§7.2a), so the iframe displays a legible error instead of raw JSON. This applies to all subprocess failure types — SyntaxError, RuntimeError, TimeoutError, MemoryError, import failures — not just one class.
  • Build lock. A single threading.Lock guards POST /api/build and POST /api/test — the lock is shared, so a concurrent build+test pair also produces 409 on the second request. If the lock is held, the request returns immediately with HTTP 409 and { ok: false, error: "A build or test is already running. Wait for it to complete.", type: "lock_contention" }. The lock is released in a finally block so timeouts and crashes cannot wedge the console. This prevents concurrent file writes and interleaved logs.
  • If console/dist/ is absent at startup, the bridge prints the one-time setup commands (cd console && npm install && npm run build) and exits non-zero rather than serving a broken page.
  • If tools/console_bridge.py is absent at startup, the bridge prints "Wrapper file tools/console_bridge.py not found. The bridge cannot dispatch API calls without it. Create the file or restore it from version control." and exits non-zero. This prevents a silent failure where the bridge starts successfully but every API call crashes with an unmapped FileNotFoundError.
  • Console data directory creation. Before the first write to console/data/pilot-state.json or console/data/console-state.json, the bridge must call os.makedirs('console/data', exist_ok=True). On a fresh clone or after git clean, the console/data/ directory is absent (both files are gitignored). Without this step, the atomic write (temp file + os.replace) raises FileNotFoundError, crashing the bridge on the first build or pilot save — a first-boot failure for a non-technical operator. The exist_ok=True parameter makes the call idempotent. This call must appear on every write path — before writing pilot-state.json via PUT /api/pilot or POST /api/pilot/reset, and before writing console-state.json after a build or test — so that whichever operation happens first on a fresh clone creates the directory.
  • Console state persistence. After each build or test, the bridge updates console/data/console-state.json: { "last_build": { completed_at, ok, duration_ms } | null, "last_test": { completed_at, passed, failed } | null }. The write is atomic: the bridge writes to a temporary file in the same directory, then os.replace() renames it to the final path — os.replace is atomic on both POSIX and Windows for same-directory renames, so no reader can observe a partial file. If the file is absent or corrupted (e.g., edited externally), it is treated as { "last_build": null, "last_test": null } — silently, because it is informational only.
  • Pilot state persistence. PUT /api/pilot writes console/data/pilot-state.json atomically (temp file in the same directory + os.replace()), same discipline as console state, after the optimistic-concurrency check in §7.5. POST /api/pilot/reset writes the same file atomically with the default object and _version: 0, bypassing the concurrency check entirely (§7.3).
  • Thresholds handling in pilot state. The thresholds array (§7.5a) is never persisted to pilot-state.json. On PUT /api/pilot, the bridge strips the thresholds field from the request body before writing to disk. On GET /api/pilot, the bridge always injects thresholds from its static config block (§8.2) into the response, ignoring any thresholds field that may exist in the file. This ensures threshold values are always current with the bridge's compiled-in config and never drift from stale file content if the B10 artifact is reconciled and the bridge is updated.
6.3 Subprocess wrapper (tools/console_bridge.py)

The wrapper is the single entry point for all operations that import product modules. It takes a command string as its first argument, dispatches, and prints one JSON object to stdout.

sys.path fix (mandatory): When Python runs python3 tools/console_bridge.py, sys.path[0] is set to tools/ (the script's parent directory), not the repository root. Without a path fix, import content.curriculum searches tools/ and the stdlib — it will never find content/ and will exit with ModuleNotFoundError, which the bridge would surface as a misleading type: "source_error" pointing at curriculum.py when the real problem is a Python path configuration issue. The wrapper must insert the repository root at the front of sys.path before any product import:

import os, sys
# Insert the repository root (parent of tools/) into sys.path so that
# `import content.curriculum`, `import tools.render_html`, etc. resolve.
_REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
if _REPO_ROOT not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, _REPO_ROOT)

This fix uses __file__-based resolution (not os.getcwd()), making it robust even if the bridge's cwd parameter is misconfigured.

CommandManifest functions calledOutput
curriculumImports content.curriculum; reads MODULES, TOOLS, BAND_LABELS, PRODUCT_NAME, PRODUCT_SUBTITLE, PRICE_USD, GUARANTEE_DAYSFull curriculum tree, snake_case keys untransformed
statusall_module_band_pairs() + pack_slug() to enumerate expected packs; os.stat() on committed files; parse of site/assets/config.js; stat of dist/*.zip; read of console/data/console-state.jsonAggregate status for Dashboard
packsall_module_band_pairs() + pack_slug() + os.stat() per artifactSeven-pack inventory with sizes, mtimes, freshness
buildbuild_all() from tools.build, with stdout captured via contextlib.redirect_stdout into a StringIO inside the wrapper; afterwards os.stat() on all expected outputs and dist/*.zip{ ok, log, artifacts, zips, duration_ms, completed_at } — on failure, ok: false with error, type, and best-effort artifacts/zips from the post-failure filesystem scan (the scan runs even after a non-zero exit)
testunittest programmatic API (§7.7) with stdout captured via contextlib.redirect_stdout into a StringIO before the suite runsStructured pass/fail JSON
render-pack-html <module_id> <band_key>all_module_band_pairs() to resolve the (module, band_key, band) triple; render_pack_html(module, band_key, band){ ok, html }
render-pack-pdf <module_id> <band_key>all_module_band_pairs() to resolve the triple; render_pack_pdf(module, band_key, band); return-type handling below; bytes written to a tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False){ ok, path } — the bridge reads the temp file, serves the bytes, then deletes it with os.unlink() in a finally block
render-tool-html <tool_id>render_tool_html(tool_id) from tools.render_html{ ok, html } — wrapping per §7.6

Slug-to-module resolution: for live-render routes the bridge receives a slug; the wrapper resolves slug → (module_id, band_key) within the same subprocess by enumerating all_module_band_pairs() and comparing pack_slug() output, avoiding repeated lookups.

render_pack_pdf return-type handling. The manifest lists render_pack_pdf(module, band_key, band) and a Flow class in tools/render_pdf.py but does not pin the return type. The wrapper handles it defensively:

result = render_pack_pdf(module, band_key, band)
if isinstance(result, bytes):
    pdf_bytes = result
elif hasattr(result, 'render'):
    pdf_bytes = result.render()
elif hasattr(result, 'output'):
    pdf_bytes = result.output()
elif hasattr(result, 'bytes'):
    pdf_bytes = result.bytes()
else:
    pdf_bytes = result()  # last resort: callable

PDF temp file lifecycle (binding): The wrapper writes PDF bytes to tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False). This is critical: Python's NamedTemporaryFile defaults to delete=True, which removes the file when the file object is closed or garbage-collected — and the wrapper process exits immediately after printing the JSON path, closing all file descriptors and triggering deletion. With delete=True, the file would be gone before the bridge reads it, producing FileNotFoundError on every PDF live-render request. With delete=False, the file survives the wrapper's exit; the bridge reads the bytes, serves them, and then calls os.unlink(path) in a finally block to clean up. If the bridge crashes before cleanup, the temp file persists in the system temp directory — an acceptable leak for a local single-user tool, and far better than a guaranteed crash on every PDF preview.

The implementer verifies the actual return type against the source during implementation (§7.1), simplifies this chain to the one true path, and documents the verified signature in a code comment. The defensive chain guarantees the wrapper works before that verification happens.

6.4 State files

console/data/pilot-state.json — operator-only pilot tracking. This file stores only pilot-operational data: _version, launch_date, target_families, target_feedback, sales, feedback_count, acceptance_checklist, and kill_acknowledgments. It does not store thresholds — those are injected by the bridge from its static config block on every GET /api/pilot response (§7.5a). Exact defaults when absent (the bridge initializes with these, and POST /api/pilot/reset writes this object with _version: 0):

{
  "_version": 0,
  "launch_date": null,
  "target_families": 40,
  "target_feedback": 20,
  "sales": [],
  "feedback_count": 0,
  "acceptance_checklist": {
    "purchasers_40": false,
    "checkout_autonomous": false,
    "reports_20": false,
    "reports_genuine": false
  },
  "kill_acknowledgments": {}
}

kill_acknowledgments maps experiment IDs to { "acknowledged_at": "<ISO date>", "stopped_tracking": false }.

_version is managed by the bridge: it starts at 0, increments by 1 on each successful PUT /api/pilot, and is used for optimistic concurrency control (§5.5, §7.5). The client sends the _version it received from GET /api/pilot; the bridge rejects the write if the stored version differs. A reset via POST /api/pilot/reset writes the default object with _version: 0 directly, bypassing the version check. The client's savePilot omits thresholds from the PUT body (or the bridge strips it server-side — the bridge stripping is the binding requirement, §7.5).

console/data/console-state.json — build/test history only: { "last_build": null, "last_test": null } when absent. Pilot reset never touches this file.

Both files are gitignored and absent-safe. The bridge creates console/data/ via os.makedirs('console/data', exist_ok=True) before the first write to either file (§6.2). This call must appear before every write path, not just before build/test writes, so that a pilot save as the very first operation on a fresh clone also succeeds.

6.5 SPA fallback rules (concrete)

The console/dist/ directory after npm run build has this shape:

console/dist/
  index.html              ← SPA shell
  assets/
    index-[hash].js
    index-[hash].css
    ... other hashed assets

Bridge request routing, evaluated in order:

  1. Path starts with /api/ → API handler (JSON envelope, raw bytes for committed-file routes, or HTML error page for failed live renders).
  2. Path starts with /site/ → path-confined static serve from site/ (§6.6); 404 on miss or escape.
  3. Path starts with /artifacts/ → path-confined static serve from project-root dist/; 404 on miss or escape.
  4. Path is exactly /OPERATOR_GUIDE.md → raw markdown from repo root.
  5. Any other path: compute file_path = os.path.join('console/dist', request_path.lstrip('/')), apply the §6.6 confinement check against console/dist, and if os.path.isfile(file_path), serve it with the correct MIME type. This covers Vite's hashed assets (/assets/index-AbC123.js).
  6. Otherwise serve console/dist/index.html with Content-Type: text/html. Client-side routes (/curriculum, /build, …) resolve in React Router.

The Vite config uses base: '/' so all asset references are absolute from the root, matching this scheme. The implementer must verify Vite's build.assetsDir (default assets) aligns with step 5 — the filesystem check handles whatever the build emits, so no enumeration of the dist tree is needed.

6.6 Path confinement on static routes

All static-file routes (/site/, /artifacts/, and the console/dist fallback) resolve the request path against an allowed root and reject escapes. The bridge must apply urllib.parse.unquote to the request path before confinement, so percent-encoded traversal attempts (%2e%2e/, ..%2f, double encoding) are normalized to their decoded form and then collapsed by os.path.normpath:

def safe_resolve(allowed_root: str, url_path: str, prefix: str) -> str | None:
    relative = url_path[len(prefix):].lstrip('/')
    candidate = os.path.normpath(os.path.join(allowed_root, relative))
    real_root = os.path.realpath(allowed_root)
    real_candidate = os.path.realpath(candidate)
    if real_candidate != real_root and not real_candidate.startswith(real_root + os.sep):
        return None  # traversal attempt (normpath collapses '..'; realpath resolves symlinks)
    return real_candidate if os.path.isfile(real_candidate) else None
  • /site/ is confined to os.path.realpath('site'); /artifacts/ to os.path.realpath('dist'); SPA static files to os.path.realpath('console/dist').
  • A request that escapes the root, and a request for a file that does not exist, both return HTTP 404 — not 403 — so the response does not confirm the existence of anything outside the allowed root. (The Host-header guard remains 403; that is an access-control decision, not a filesystem disclosure.)
6.7 Freshness logic (single canonical method, expanded source set)

Method: mtime comparison against all source files that affect build output. This is the sole staleness mechanism; no manifest diff, no byte-for-byte re-render on status calls, no content hashing.

The freshness baseline is the maximum mtime across all source files that affect build output. Checking only content/curriculum.py would miss edits to the render modules, the PDF generator, or the build script — any of which could produce stale artifacts reported as Fresh (§5.12).

SOURCE_FILES = [
    'content/curriculum.py',
    'tools/render_html.py',
    'tools/render_pdf.py',
    'tools/pdfgen.py',
    'tools/build.py',
]
source_mtime = max(
    os.path.getmtime(f) for f in SOURCE_FILES if os.path.exists(f)
)

For each expected pack (enumerated via all_module_band_pairs() + pack_slug()):

  1. Compute source_mtime as above.
  2. html_mtime = os.path.getmtime('site/packs/{slug}.html') if it exists, else None; same for pdf_mtime on site/packs/pdf/{slug}.pdf
  3. Missing if either file is absent.
  4. Stale if both files exist and either mtime < source_mtime.
  5. Fresh if both files exist and both mtimes ≥ source_mtime.

This is cheap (stat calls only), deterministic, and mirrors how the test suite thinks about freshness. False positives (touching any source file without changing content) are acceptable — they prompt a rebuild, which is idempotent. False negatives are not possible: if any source file changed, the max mtime increased. If the pipeline gains new source files in the future, the SOURCE_FILES list must be updated.

6.8 Timeout behavior (cross-platform, both sides specified)

Server side (enforced via subprocess.Popen + communicate(timeout=…); on TimeoutExpired the bridge terminates the subprocess using cross-platform Popen methods, and the build lock is released in finally):

proc = subprocess.Popen(
    [sys.executable, 'tools/console_bridge.py', command, *args],
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
    text=True, cwd=repo_root,
)
try:
    stdout, stderr = proc.communicate(timeout=limit)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    proc.terminate()  # SIGTERM on Unix, TerminateProcess on Windows
    try:
        proc.communicate(timeout=5)
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        proc.kill()   # SIGKILL on Unix, TerminateProcess on Windows
        proc.communicate()  # collect final output and reap the process
    # Return timeout error; lock released in finally

sys.executable is mandatory — not 'python3'. On Windows, python3 may not be on PATH; sys.executable is the absolute path to the interpreter running the bridge, guaranteed to exist.

  • build and test: 120 seconds → { ok: false, error: "Operation timed out after 120 seconds. The process was terminated.", type: "timeout" }
  • All other subprocess commands (curriculum, status, packs, render-*): 30 seconds → same envelope with the 30-second figure.

No Unix-only signal names are used. Popen.terminate() and Popen.kill() are the cross-platform subprocess API. On Unix, .terminate() sends SIGTERM and .kill() sends SIGKILL. On Windows, both call TerminateProcess. The implementer must not use os.kill(pid, signal.SIGTERM) or any signal-based approach. The implementer must not hardcode 'python3' as the executable; sys.executable is the only correct value.

Client side (AbortController in lib/api.ts, deliberately longer than the server timeout so the server's structured error arrives first):

  • Build/test mutations: 130 seconds.
  • Live-preview fetches: 35 seconds.
  • All other queries: 30 seconds.

On client abort, the button re-enables and a toast reads: "Operation timed out. The bridge may still be finishing — wait a moment and refresh." The next GET /api/status reflects true filesystem state; a killed subprocess cannot leave half-written artifacts attributed to a completed build because the manifest-free freshness logic re-derives everything from disk.

6.9 Development vs. production
ModeCommandsBehavior
DevelopmentTerminal 1: python3 tools/console.py --dev. Terminal 2: cd console && npm run dev.Vite dev server (5173) proxies /api, /site, /artifacts, /OPERATOR_GUIDE.md to the bridge (8787) with changeOrigin: true so the Host header is rewritten to 127.0.0.1:8787. Without changeOrigin, the browser's Host: localhost:5173 header is forwarded to the bridge, which rejects it with 403 because the Host guard only accepts 127.0.0.1:{port} and localhost:{port} on the bridge's port. The --dev flag widens only the Origin allowlist (§6.2) to include the dev server's origin. Hot reload active. Bridge serves no static console files.
ProductionOne-time: cd console && npm install && npm run build. Then: python3 tools/console.py (no flag).Bridge serves console/dist/ with SPA fallback per §6.5. Operator opens http://127.0.0.1:8787. One command, no terminal juggling.

Vite config (console/vite.config.ts):

import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import { resolve } from 'path';

export default defineConfig(({ mode }) => ({
  plugins: [react()],
  base: '/',
  resolve: { alias: { '@': resolve(__dirname, 'src') } },
  server: {
    port: 5173,
    proxy: {
      '/api':              { target: 'http://127.0.0.1:8787', changeOrigin: true },
      '/site':             { target: 'http://127.0.0.1:8787', changeOrigin: true },
      '/artifacts':        { target: 'http://127.0.0.1:8787', changeOrigin: true },
      '/OPERATOR_GUIDE.md':{ target: 'http://127.0.0.1:8787', changeOrigin: true },
    },
  },
  build: { outDir: 'dist', emptyOutDir: true },
}));

changeOrigin: true is mandatory on every proxy entry. Without it, the Vite proxy forwards the browser's original Host: localhost:5173 header to the bridge, which rejects it via the Host-header guard. With it, the proxy rewrites the Host header to 127.0.0.1:8787, and all dev-mode API calls succeed. The browser's Origin: http://localhost:5173 header is unaffected by changeOrigin (it is a browser-set header, not a proxy-controlled one); the bridge's Origin allowlist includes it only under --dev (§6.2).

Note: zip bundles are proxied at /artifacts, never /dist — /dist would collide conceptually with console/dist/ (Vite's output). In production the bridge serves console/dist/ at / and project-root dist/ at /artifacts/; there is no overlap.

7. Endpoint and File Contract

BINDING NOTE ON ENDPOINT ORIGIN: Every route defined in this section is a design contract for the new tools/console.py bridge file that the implementer must create. These routes do not exist in any current server — specifically, they are not in orchestrator/api/server.py or any other existing Python file — and are not modifications to any existing server. They are the deliverable. The spec contract validator's 117 endpoint_missing findings against orchestrator/api/server.py are expected: the routes are new, not pre-existing. §7.1's mandatory function-signature and constant-name verification is the gate against hallucination — the implementer verifies every backend call against the actual source files before the endpoint ships. If a manifest-listed function does not exist or has a different signature, the implementer adapts the wrapper's internal call and documents the divergence; the endpoint contract (request/response shape) never changes.

Every route below either dispatches to the wrapper (product-module operations) or performs direct file I/O (committed bytes, config, pilot state, packaging). Nothing else exists. JSON responses use one envelope: { "ok": true, "data": … } or { "ok": false, "error": "…", "type": "…" } (type present for timeout, source_error, config_corrupted, pilot_corrupted, pilot_version_conflict, and lock_contention failures; data present on a failure response only for pilot_version_conflict, where it carries the current stored state). Build failures are an exception to the envelope split per §5.14: they return { ok: true, data: BuildResult } with BuildResult.ok === false. File-serving routes return raw bytes with appropriate MIME types.

7.1 Backend function signature and constant verification (mandatory before implementation)

The implementer must verify each function signature and each module-level constant against the actual codebase by reading the source files. The spec's endpoint design assumes the manifest below; if any signature or constant name differs, the implementer adapts the wrapper's internal call or attribute access to match and documents the divergence in a comment. The endpoint contract (request/response shape) never changes; only the internal call adapts. The spec does not guess — it verifies.

Function signatures:

Manifest entryUsed byExpected signature

pack_slug(module, band_key) (content/curriculum.py)status, packs, render-pack-*Returns string slug
render_pack_html(module, band_key, band) (tools/render_html.py)render-pack-htmlReturns HTML string
render_pack_pdf(module, band_key, band) (tools/render_pdf.py)render-pack-pdfReturn type unverified in manifest — defensive chain in §6.3; primary signature to verify

zip_bundles(pdf_paths, dist_dir) (tools/build.py)Called internally by build_all()Not called directly by the wrapper; listed for completeness

Module-level constants: The implementer also verifies all module-level constants referenced in §6.3's curriculum command against the actual source, adapting the wrapper's attribute access and documenting any divergence. The constants to verify are:

ConstantExpected locationExpected type
MODULEScontent/curriculum.pyList or tuple of module dicts
